prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat electronic bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: I keep magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene as my preferred configuration, and I have tested that choice against B019 more seriously this round than in round 1. What decides it for me is the criterion I apply to every candidate: an original, experimentally verified discovery that opens a door to phenomena nobody could reach before. Here a quantitative prediction (Bistritzer and MacDonald, 2011) said where to look, and the 2018 transport experiments found correlated insulating and superconducting states at that angle. That is a number predicted and then seen, and the phenomena have since been reproduced in many independent laboratories and extended to a whole family of moire systems, including states found later such as fractional Chern insulators. That later survival is a better stability test than the exact shape of the superconducting dome. The pairing mechanism is a follow-up question; it does not change what was discovered, and the Prize has never required that the explanation be closed. I also do not think waiting is neutral, because the record of who did what is clean today and gets harder to separate as the field grows. Three names fit exactly the prediction and the first experiment.
statement.case_against: My own objections have not gone away. The credit is the weak point: the 2018 measurements were made by Yuan Cao, Valla Fatemi and other junior coauthors in Jarillo-Herrero's group, and I cannot be absolutely sure that naming the group leader alone is the right allocation for the experimental half. The pairing mechanism is unsettled and twist-angle disorder limits quantitative comparison between devices. The field is eight years old, which is young by this committee's standards. B019 is the mature and cleanly attributed alternative, and my round-1 colleagues are right that its interpretation is closed and its uncertainty budgets are agreed across institutes. My hesitation about B019 is a different one and a narrow one: Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and first demonstration are the original invention, but the committee must be sure that Ye is credited for original work and not for doing the later, better experiment, because the rule is that the Prize goes to the original experiment and not to the second discoverer who did it better. If the priority record shows that Ye's contribution is a distinct step (many-body clocks and the 1e-18 systematic budget), I would regard B019 as fully defensible and would not oppose it.

responses.point: Kroll holds that the lattice clock is a new measurement capability and not a refinement, because the magic wavelength removes the lattice light shift so many atoms can be interrogated at once, and he asks that the citation name the magic-wavelength concept explicitly.
responses.response: I accept that answer to the chair's question: what is new is the invention of the magic-wavelength trap, which is a different thing from the comb or the single-ion work, and the Prize is for a discovery or an invention, so it does qualify. I agree the citation should rest on the instrument and its physics and leave the redefinition of the second out. My remaining point is attribution rather than science: if the concept and first demonstration are Katori's, the committee needs to say in the record what Ye added that is original and not an improvement. Until that priority check on the first Sr lattice clock is done, I cannot be absolutely sure the pair is the right one, even though I agree it is the cleanest allocation on the shortlist.

responses.point: Pearce says he would move B047 up if the experimental attribution could be defended, since Jarillo-Herrero is the group leader while Cao and Fatemi made the measurements, but would not put it ahead of B019 this year.
responses.response: My defence is a modest one. The twist-angle experiment was the group's own programme, guided by the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction, and the committee has regularly credited the person who conceived and led the original experiment when the three-name limit prevents naming the junior authors. I do not claim this removes the cost: Cao and Fatemi are real omissions and I would have the record say so plainly. Where I differ from you is on timing. The discovery and its reproduction are established, and the open mechanism question belongs to later work, so I do not think a clean interpretation of the clocks should automatically put them ahead of a verified discovery whose credited names are checkable.

responses.point: Lindroth asks what new evidence in the next two or three years would change my view about stability, and whether the three-name set including Bistritzer survives the objection that experimental credit sits with junior authors.
responses.response: Evidence that would change my view would be a finding that the correlated and superconducting phases depend on a particular fabrication route or on disorder in a way that cannot be reproduced across groups; so far the opposite is true, and the persistence of the phenomenology in other moire systems is the point I weigh most. On the set, Bistritzer survives because the magic-angle result is the Bistritzer-MacDonald paper, and a prize that credits the prediction should name both authors. The junior-author problem I cannot repair within three names, but it is a gap in the allocation that I would state openly, not a reason to doubt that the discovery is real.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect for their fifteen years of independent confirmation, and would credit only MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero in B047.
responses.response: I take your maturity argument seriously, and it is the best argument for B012, which stays my second alternative. But the credit gap there is the harder one: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe route that Molenkamp realised, Zhang has died, and a citation restricted to the 2D quantum spin Hall effect still has the overlap with the 2016 prize to be settled. For B047 I still disagree with dropping Bistritzer; with three names the prediction and the experiment are both represented and I would be unwilling to leave out someone who did part of the original work.

uncertainties: Whether naming Jarillo-Herrero alone on the experimental side is acceptable when Cao, Fatemi and other 2018 coauthors made the measurements.
Whether the priority record for the first Sr lattice clock (Katori, JILA, SYRTE) would show Ye's contribution to be a distinct original step, which bears on whether B019 should come first.
Whether the committee regards the unsettled pairing mechanism as a reason to wait or only as a follow-up question.
Whether parallel moire work by other groups needs a priority check before the final ballot.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with any shortlisted candidate or credited name is apparent from my profile; my frequent coauthors and mentors are not among them. I note only that Goran Johansson is also at Chalmers Physics and that Mehlig is at the neighbouring Gothenburg department, which does not bear on B047, B019 or B012. My field is electron microscopy of materials, so I judge the condensed-matter and clock candidates on the experimental record and not as an expert in either.
